significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish both a form-(ii) causal decomposition—"steering these features independently modulates belief-attribution and factual-assertion behavior"—and a form-(iii) predictive coupling whereby feature "entanglement ... predicts behavioral conflation" across checkpoints. This mechanism-plus-phenomenon conclusion would predict which models or training stages confuse belief with fact, a consequential constraint given that SAE work such as Templeton et al. (2024) treats causal feature interventions as useful while documenting imperfect feature specificity. A negative result would undermine SAE-feature entanglement as the explanation, although it would not rule out separation in representations that an SAE failed to recover; true and false outcomes are distinguishable despite the weakly quantified phrase "largely disjoint." After substituting only the general LLM-beliefs topic, I would not retain this score: the cross-checkpoint entanglement–behavior coupling and two-way causal separation are specific additions beyond the topic-median probe-and-steer hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "entanglement metric" as a diagnostic or predictor and "clamping the belief-attribution feature" as an intervention; because entanglement is claimed to predict later benchmark conflation, the metric can operate ex ante, whereas steering is a model-specific mitigation lever. Individual features would require re-extraction on each model, but the claimed relation survives recalibration by predicting that checkpoints with greater recovered feature overlap will exhibit greater behavioral conflation. The asserted scope covers "model sizes and instruction-tuning stages," supporting uptake by interpretability researchers and model auditors, but it does not claim transfer across architectures, modalities, or deployment domains. Topic substitution would remove both the predictor and intervention and therefore would not justify this score; their presence gives the claim more reach than a generic study of LLM beliefs.
